definition: Computational geometry is a branch of computer science devoted to the study of algorithms that can be stated in terms of geometry.
details: Some purely geometrical problems arise out of the study of computational geometric algorithms, and such problems are also considered to be part of computational geometry. While modern computational geometry is a recent development, it is one of the oldest fields of computing with a history stretching back to antiquity. Computational complexity is central to computational geometry, with great practical significance if algorithms are used on very large datasets containing tens or hundreds of millions of points. For such sets, the difference between O(n2) and O(n log n) may be the difference between days and seconds of computation. The main impetus for the development of computational geometry as a discipline was progress in computer graphics and computer-aided design and manufacturing (CAD/CAM), but many problems in computational geometry are classical in nature, and may come from mathematical visualization. Other important applications of computational geometry include robotics (motion planning and visibility problems), geographic information systems (GIS) (geometrical location and search, route planning), integrated circuit design (IC geometry design and verification), computer-aid

explainer.lead: Computational geometry turns questions about points, lines and shapes into algorithms a computer can run efficiently. It matters in tasks such as planning robot motion, searching maps and designing chips, especially when a slower algorithm could take days instead of seconds.

tiers.eli5: Imagine trying to find the quickest route through a huge drawing full of roads and obstacles. Computational geometry is about teaching a computer clever ways to solve puzzles involving points, lines and shapes. A clever method can finish much faster than checking every possible pair or path.
tiers.practitioner: In robotics, GIS, CAD/CAM and chip design, geometric algorithms should be chosen for their scaling behaviour as well as their correctness. A quadratic method may be impractical on tens or hundreds of millions of points, while an O(n log n) method can make the same class of task dramatically faster. Typical problems include motion planning, visibility, geometric search, route planning and IC geometry verification.
tiers.paperLevel: Computational geometry studies algorithms that can be stated in geometric terms, together with their computational complexity; purely geometric problems arising from this study also fall within the field. Scaling is central: for very large n, the difference between O(n^2) and O(n log n) can mean days rather than seconds of computation. The modern discipline was driven largely by computer graphics and CAD/CAM, although many of its problems are classical and its history reaches back to antiquity.

explainer.example: Suppose a geographic information system must process 100 million points. An O(n^2) approach and an O(n log n) approach may both be correct, but their running times can differ from days to seconds, making algorithm choice decisive.

explainer.intuition: Many computing tasks are really questions about geometric objects and their relationships. Computational geometry finds efficient procedures for answering those questions and studies how their cost grows with input size.
howItWorks: State the task in terms of geometric objects, such as points or shapes.
Identify the required result, such as a route, location or visibility answer.
Design an algorithm that uses the geometry rather than blindly examining every possibility.
Analyse its computational complexity, especially for very large inputs.
Apply it in areas such as graphics, robotics, GIS or chip design.
explainer.whyItMatters: Correctness alone is not enough when geometric datasets contain tens or hundreds of millions of points. Efficient algorithms make practical work in graphics, manufacturing, robotics, mapping and integrated circuit design possible at these scales.
misconceptions: It is not merely the use of geometric formulas; it centres on algorithms and their complexity.
It is not an entirely new subject: the modern discipline is recent, but its problems and history reach back to antiquity.
A correct algorithm is not necessarily practical for very large geometric datasets.
